What would be thought of the Minister of Railways, for instance, if all the engineers on the Intercolonial railway, from Montreal to Sydney were on strike, and in the middle of that strike, the Minister of Railways should go to England? Yet, when this difficulty arose in British Columbia, originating in two collieries and extending to all the labour, interests of British Columbia-for it was not confined to the miners but extended to other sections of labour as well-this of all times was the one the minister chose for his holiday. Is it any wonder that the public, whether labouring men, employers or men who view public affairs only in a most casual way, were shocked that, under these circumstances, the minister should desert his post? I am sure the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) would not have done it. True, he allows steamers to go off carrying flour barrels with whisky in them. He says he does not know about that, but I think he has a shrewd suspicion as to what was going on. I will say this for the Minister of Customs, that he is usually on his job. But it was apparently not so with the Minister of Labour. Compare this with what was done in England. There they had coal strikes and threatened railway strikes. Did ministerial gentlemen of that country hold their hands in supine content? Did they run away from the country? The Prime Minister of Great Britain summoned to his aid the most active of his colleagues, treated by intercession with the different interests involved, to save the country from the difficulty which would arise through the stoppage of the coal supplies and of the railways. It does not seem to make any difference to the Minister of Labour whether the miners of British Columbia have work or not, whether the artisans in other lines of labour are employed or not, whether the business men of that country have to import coal from the United States or not. He was in England, enjoying himself with the Unionists of that country. No doubt, sitting at the table of the Carlton Club or some other organization of the kind, the hon. gentleman over his good dinner never thought for a moment of these men, who, exasperated by their sense of wrong were fighting for what they deemed, rightly or wrongly, to be their rights. Such thoughts were not for the minister; he was on his jaunting tour and proposed to have his fun. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) went out to British Columbia, and I believe a picket stopped him somewhere. But, so far as he is concerned, the mention 
of that incident is the only one to show that he ever gave the slightest thought to this question involving the welfare of the labouring men of British Columbia and the business interests so seriously affected by that strike.
I now come to my solemn and intellectual friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty). He jaunted out to British Columbia. Has anybody told us that he applied his intellect to an attempt to solve this problem as to how labour and capital could be reconciled? So far, there is no glimmer of such an idea. One minister was in England-the responsible minister-others were everywhere else. Two of them happened to go into the country where this strike existed, but they did not bother their heads about it. Is it any wonder that the labouring people of British Columbia reached the point where they had no respect for this Government or for the men composing it? And that is why the strike is on.
Now, we have the report of Mr. Price who was sent out as commissioner. I do not know the gentleman, but I agree with my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) in his criticism of the selection made. Coal miners are a class of workingmen whose sense of justice, whose desire for remedies for the problems of labour, are peculiar to themselves. And so, though the hon. minister's late partner may have been a most estimable man, I do not think that the fact that he had had some experience in regard to miners in Cobalt fitted him for the work he was called upon to do in this case. Every one familiar with these matters knows that there is a great difference between the coal miners and the gold miners in their conceptions of labour conditions. The hon. minister should have come to Nova Scotia or should have gone to British Columbia, to find a man, who knew what were the coal miners' conceptions of right and justice. Had he selected some one familiar with the ideals of these men and with the methods adopted by employers in dealing with these questions, instead of taking his former law partner, he would have had one whose opinions would have commanded more respect among the men and in that way might possibly have reached a solution of this diffficulty.
We have heard a good deal about the former Minister of Labour, and the question of what he did or did not do. I notice in his report the commissioner tells what Mr. Mackenzie King did on one occasion deal-

mg with the same conditions in the West as were involved in this strike. He says:
In 1905, trouble occurred at the mines of the "Western Fuel Company, arising out of an order of the company requiring the men to provide their own transportation to a shaft where they could enter in nearer proximity to the place of work. This order was said to have been by reason of the enforcement of the provincial law limiting the hours of underground labour to eight hours a day, bank to bank. As usually happens in such cases. Other differences were also presented after the trouble arose, and the recognition of the United Mine Workers' union, to which a number of the miners then belonged, was also demanded. With the assistance of the then Deputy Minister of Labour, Mr. W. L. Mackenzie King, the matter was finally adjusted between a committee of the men and the mine management, and an agreement entered into between the company and the men which with some alterations, has continued down to the time of the present strike.
Dealing with exactly the same conditions and exactly the same problems, the commissioner whom my hon. friend sends out to British Columbia comes back and gives us evidence that the late Minister of Labour knew how to deal with these problems and succeeded in bringing industrial peace to that part of the country. We need no further evidence as to this; I presume my hon. friend the Minister of Labour and his followers will not question the finding of their own commissioner upon that point.
There is another interesting finding here in which I happen to have a very great personal interest. I remember being in this House when the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act was passed, and I remember the election which followed. In my constituency we have eight or nine coal mines in operation,' and one thing for which I was bitterly attacked during that election campaign was that the Government which I had supported had undertaken to pass a piece of legislation which would take away from the labouring man the right to strike. Orators, party leaders, like the present leader of the Conservative party in the provincial House, who was my opponent in that election, shouted all over the constituency about the horrible treatment that had been accorded to the labouring men by the Liberal Government. One would have thought that this Government upon taking office would have hastened to the task of sweeping this iniquitous piece of legislation off the statute book. Every man on this side of the House who represents a constituency in which there are labouring men, remembers that he had to
pass through the same ordeal. If this Government came in committed to anything other than the Halifax platform, which they have forgotten all about, it was that this Lemieux Labour Act, as it was called, would be repealed. The hon. member for Vancouver does not want it repealed; he wants it made tighter; he wants compulsory arbitration. But here is the opinion of the commissioner:
I believe that the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, notwithstanding defects, which could hardly be hoped would be avoided in its earlier history, is a very beneficial Act, not only in the interest of the general public, but also in the interest, ultimately, at all events, of both employees and employers as well.
I wanted to get that assertion on 'Hansard'; this Conservative Minister of Labour having sent out his own confidant to investigate labour conditions in this country, I wanted to put on record the deliberate opinion of his commissioner as to the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. I want to have it established that the stories told by Conservative orators in 1908 were all moonshine, and that this Industrial Disputes Investigation Act is a very beneficial Act. Out of the mouths of our enemies comes this praise of that piece of legislation passed by the Liberal Government in 1907. For two years hon, gentlemen opposite have been in power, and the Minister of Labour has allowed that Act to remain on the statute book untouched and unaltered even in the slightest degree. To argue the question as to whether or not the principle of this Act is a matter for which we on this side of the House have to make any defence to-day seems to me, in view of the position adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite at this stage, to be entirely unnecessary. But the hon. member for Vancouver has told us that the minister is contemplating some amendments to the Act; it will be interesting to see what those amendments are. I observe that the commissioner has given us some suggestions; these are the amendments he wants us to make:
In order that there may be no room for
doubt in the mind of any one as to what is forbidden by it, I think the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act should be amended, especially the definition of 'strike' and section 56, so as to clearly cover what Is in reality a strike or lockout, and make the provisions of the law more easily understood and more likely to be properly enforced.
That is a rather general recommendation, and it is somewhat difficult to see on the

face of it what its effect would be. He goes on to say:
Without any further comment upon the practice of calling cessation of work a * holiday,' or reflecting on the hona fides of the contention that the men at Cumberland and Ladysmith believed they were not offending against the law in what they did, it will be recognized that it is desirable and very important that this work should be made plain.
That apparently is a proposed amendment of the law intended distinctly to militate against the interests of the labour men. If that recommendation made by Mr. Price means anything, it is intended further to confine and limit the right of labour men under this Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. Here is another one :	-
I think it should he made clear by special prohibition, under penalty, that it is unlawful to practice any kind of intimidation, abuse or insult against any one or to publish, call or refer to any one as a ' scab ' or ' blackleg ' or as unfair to labour or to incite or threaten to do any of these things, with a view to influencing the acts of any person in connection with any strike or labour dispute.
Does the commissioner mean that we should have legislation absolutely prohibiting the right to picket? I remember being in the Imperial Parliament some six or seven years ago and, sitting in the gallery, hearing a discussion on the labour legislation proposed by the Liberal Government of that day, in which the right to picket was expressly recognized by statute; I think that is on the statute book of the mother country still. So far as I can judge from the report made by Mr. Price, his recommendations in regard to this matter are all intended to militate against the rights of labour men. His report is a very nice, academic essay upon labour questions generally, written too late in some respects, but all too soon in others. When the minister went to England, why did he not instruct Mr. Price to remain o'n the ground and investigate conditions after the riot? Why did he instruct him to fold up his portmanteau, come back to Ottawa and write his report when the most crucial point in the whole matter had been reached? The short time he spent in considering the matter and two weeks' deliberation on the part of the minister in regard to the industrial conflict which has now lasted for a year and four months is the only evidence we have that the minister bothered his head about the subject. Is it any wonder that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House raise questions in regard to this matter? Is it any wonder that when my hon. friend asks us for money to carry
[Mr. Macdonald. 1
on the affairs of his department we should take advantage of the occasion to arraign him for his incompetency in dealing with these matters? I think that those of us who represent constituencies wherein labouring men are employed, as well as those who represent constituencies where the interests of capital are concerned, would be recreant in our duty if we did not point out that the administration of this Government, after two and a half years of trial, has been marked by incompetency and absolute failure even to give any thought to the serious problems which have arisen throughout the country. For a year and four months in the great western province of British Columbia, not only have the labouring men suffered under conditions which have called forth protests from their representatives all over the country, but the business interests of the country as well have been paralyzed, and the conditions that exist in that province are wholly and largely due to the failure of this ministry and this Government to grapple with the serious situation which has arisen.

The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has expressed a burning desire to have pointed out to him conditions parallel to those which he has been describing during the last halfhour. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) also expressed a desire to have pointed out to him any conditions at all similar to those which have prevailed on Vancouver Island for several months.

What I asked the hon.
member for Vancouver was if he could point to conditions as extraordinary as those in the province of British Columbia.

That is about what I said. As my hon. friend's request seems legitimate, I shall, even at this late hour, try to give him some facts showing a parallel case. In 1909-10 there was a strike amongst the coal miners of Nova Scotia extending over twenty-two months, seven months at Glace Bay, seven months at Inverness, and twenty-two months at Springhill. The militia were called out at Glace Bay, Spring-hill and Inverness. My hon. friend from Pictou was a member of this House. It is not on record that he suggested any amendment to this Act to meet the situation. That situation was obtaining in his own province, within a stone's throw of his own door. He was in this House but did nothing. I would not, by substantive motion,

find any fault with him for not taking any action but I am simply trying to gratify his burning desire for a parallel case. Perhaps the hon. member from Cape Breton was at Glace Bay at that time. It is not on record that' he did anything to settle the strike that was on at Glace Bay for about seven months or to expel the militia from Glace Bay. They were sent there by the preceding Government.
Would the hon. gentleman like to know what I did?
Perhaps I had better go on now.
Perhaps you had better.

It is too bad that the hon. member for Pictou did not enlighten the House as to what he did in those conditions in Nova Scotia. If he had been in a position to tell the House that on that occasion, in order to bring about peace at Glace Bay and Inverness and Springhill where the militia had been out, he did something as a member of this House, he would have been in a better position to find fault with me for not introducing any legislation last session. He never heard of such a thing as a minister of labour leaving this country when things were in such a condition. When the strike was on, when the militia were at Glace Bay and Inverness and Springhill, my predecessor spent two months of his time in Europe.
And there was no criticism from anybody for doing it.

No. Hon. gentlemen
opposite seem to have short memories or not to desire to exercise the memories they have. I hope the hon. member for Pictou will not make so much noise again in insisting on somebody telling him that there was a parallel case some time, somewhere that occurred in his own province. According to his own remarks the circumstances convict him of having folded his arms when his fellow citizens were suffering the penalties which were inflicted on them by the militia sent there by the preceding Government.
Is the minister really in earnest when he says that the preceding Government sent the militia to Glace Bay?

The militia went to
Glace Bay. They were there.
You want to be fair.

Everybody knows
how the militia got there, we did not send the militia to Vancouver Island.
Certainly not; nobody said you did.

They were there, and nothing was done by the preceding Government by way of legislation, and nothing was done by the hon. member for Edmonton, who would like to hear of a parallel case to-night, although he was a member of the Government at that time-and nothing was done by the hon. member for Pictou to allay the suffering and the want that existed in his own native province during twenty-two months. I think we have been perhaps a little premature in this discussion to-night, although it might as well have come to-night as any time; but I may refer the House to the fact that the right hon. leader of the Opposition has a notice on the Order Paper calling for a copy of all letters, telegrams and other documents issued by any department ot this Government in respect to the strike on Vancouver Island. It is something like putting the cart before the horse to spend hours in discussing matters when many who have spoken do not know the facts and have made statement after statement that has no firmer bottom to rest on than base and discreditable insinuations. 'It. would be much more in order to wait until we get the documents before the House and then discuss the question on the facts brought forward by these documents. The hon. member for Pictou raised one or two points, that I may refer to. Mr. Price had had seven years' experience as Mining Commissioner. He was appointed after he had resigned from that position by the Government of Ontario to look into the question of" the eight hour movement, and he spent a year on that, not only in metalliferous mines, but in coal mines, and he got to know a lot.

What coal mines
are there in Ontario?
He did not remain in Ontario.
Where?
I do not remember; but outside of Ontario.
I would like to know where.
I can tell you when I see him and ask him.
But you cannot tell me.
How dare you say that when I say I can tell you. He did inquire into the length of hours in coal mines as well as in metalliferous mines.
Was he ever in one?

I think I have been
as deep in a coal mine as ever my hon. friend was.
You are deep in it now.

Hon. gentlemen opposite have seen fit to make a concerted attack upon the Department of Labour. Let me tell them a thing or two that they do not seem to know. During the first year I was in charge of the department the number of days lost in strikes was nine hundred thousand less than the year before, only about one-half the number of days lost in strikes that were lost the year before. When I was placed in charge of the department I found that the labouring men were finding a good deal of fault about delays in the operation of the Act, the length of time that elapsed between the application for conciliation boards and their appointment. I took the matter up at once and gave instructions that no unnecessary delay should be permitted, with the result that the number of days spent between the receipt of an application for a board and the establishment of the board was reduced less than one-half. In the first year I had charge of the Labour Department the average number of days between the application and the establishment of the board was seven days. The average time that elapsed during the previous year was fifteen days.
Does the minister include the Canadian Pacific railway freight handlers' strike in that category?

I am glad my hon.
friend has mentioned that particular strike. He spoke about it last year.

And you settled it up
about four days afterwards.

And he said, amongst other things, that they had made an application that year and it had not been granted. I think the leader of the Opposition also said on that occasion that it was the duty of the Minister of Labour, on application being made to him in due form, to establish a board without further delay- that it was an administrative office 'hnd not

a judicial one. The facts are that the application to which he referred was dated on the 14th day of August, 1911, and hon. gentlemen will remember, and remember for a long time, that the election occurred on the 21st day of September, and that we came into power on the 10th day of October. That application, made on the 14th of August, did not reach the Labour Department until some days afterwards; but on the 23rd day of September, two days after the election and seventeen days before we came into power, the Department of Labour refused to grant that very same labour organization a board.

Now tell us what you
did.

I will tell you what I did with respect to that particular matter. My attention having been called to it, upon going over the evidence I made up my mind that a board ought to be granted and a board was issued, or at least a settlement was effected with the men and they consented to our not proceeding.

After this has been
brought up in Parliament.

No, before it was
brought up in Parliament. That was not brought up in Parliament that I remember of. The hon. member tried to attach it to the other application but not to the one that was made to me. There were two applications made by this association. An application was made and on the 23rd September, 1911, seventeen days before we came into power, my predecessor refused that same association a board. They made another application to me but I do not think it is necessary to go into that as it has all been explained before.
In regard to this Vancouver Island strike, it has been said over and over again, and repeated here to-night, that the strike at Cumberland was caused by reason of two men being dismissed because they had reported that gas was found in a certain mine. That is not true, it never was true and I hope it will not be repeated.
That is what they allege.

That is what somebody alleges in this House.
Sir WILFRiD LAURIER: That is what the men alleged.

Did any of the men
allege that to my friend? .

Not to me,
but to my hon. friend. That is what I find in the report.
What do they report?

A letter was written by the Minister of Labour to Mr. Peter McNiven. As the hon. gentleman stated, Mr. McNiven had ceased to be in office but he received an answer from the acting secretary at Cumberland as follows:
Hon. T. W. Crothers,
Minister of Labour.
There is no strike declared at Cumberland mines. The company have openly discriminated against men who were taking an active part in union organization.
That does not answer the question at all.
Yes.

No, what I said was that it had been stated in this House, and repeated over and over again, that two men had been discriminated against because they had reported gas in that mine. There is no truth whatever in that. As a matter of fact, the two men who ceased to work for the company were one Mottishaw and one Smith. The two men who were on the gas committee were Mottishaw and Portrey and the man who wrote the report reporting gas in the mine was Portrey. Portrey, the man who wrote the report, and a member of the committee, was working for the company right up to the strike. He continued right along. It is true that Mottishaw, the other member of the committee, though not directly, was substantially dismissed; I will admit that. If they had been dismissed upon the ground alleged Portrey would have gone too. Portrey was really the man who made the report. It was written by his own hand; yet, he continued to work for the company. I think that is pretty strong evidence that they were not dismissed because they reported the existence of gas in the mines. Mr. Price finds in his report that they were not dismissed for that reason.
One of the hon. gentlemen who spoke referred to the charge that the mine owners on Vancouver Island had sent to England and secured a number of employees in Durham by fraud and misrepresentation. My hon. friend from Carleton is very familar with these words. The facts are that the Department of the Interior appointed an immigration agent at Vancouver to inquire into some charges that were made against an employment agent
in Vancouver, and during the progress of his investigation a number of these miners who were brought out from England gave evidence under oath. I have had the advantage of reading the evidence of these men. I have the evidence right in my desk here. Five of these men who were brought out declared before Mr. Reid, the immigration officer at Vancouver, that there was no misrepresentation whatever made to them in England, that when they got to Cumberland they found conditions exactly as they had been represented to them in England, and even better. It is said that some of the others jointly signed an affidavit in Vancouver to say that they had been deceived. It is only fair to state that. There were a number of them in Vancouver, they were being taken care of by the labour organization and the labour leaders were in the room and in their presence these men signed the affidavit one after the other. Some of those who signed that- affidavit gave evidence under oath before Mr. Reid and stated that they were under the care and protection of these men and that if they refused to sign that affidavit they would not get any more shelter or food. I am not stating that they were not deceived in England, but I am stating that there is plenty of evidence touching that, because five of them who testified under oath stated that they found conditions, when they reached Cumberland, better than those which had been described to them in England. The question arose in this way: The company at that time was working the mine and putting out about 60 per cent of the normal oqtput. These men who gave this testimony stated that they were told in England that there had been labour trouble at Cumberland but that they had got some men from other places and some of those who had gone on strike were returning, and that they were putting out 60 per cent of the normal output. They also said that they believed in England that they were justified in coming and working in these mines, that they had come and that they were not deceived in any respect. Others stated differently, signing this affidavit in Vancouver to which I have referred. It was stated by the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Cafroll), that an officer of the labour union had made a statement to the effect that I had refused to establish a board. To this day I have never been requested to establish a board in connection with the dispute on Vancouver Island. I requested the parties who were interested in it to apply for a board-the

miners, the mine owners and those who did not belong to a union. They all refused to do it. These gentlemen never asked me to appoint a board under the Act. They did come in one day and suggest that the men were willing to appoint a man if I would appoint a man and let the two go and inquire into the matter without any reference to the mine owners themselves. I never promised to do even that. I remember very well talking to these men and saying at a certain time that I would even at that late hour appoint a board if any one would apply for it.
In the meantime the Court of Appeal of the province of Quebec had given judgment to the effect that I had no jurisdiction to establish a board in a dispute between men who had gone on strike and former employers, because the Act applied only to disputes between employees and their employers, and as these men were no longer in the employ of their former employers, they were not in a position to ask for a board.
What case is that?

The Montreal Street
Railway case. My predecessor established a board in that case, and a prohibition was -applied for and the judge in the first instance refused the prohibition, but there was an appeal and the Court of Appeal of the province of Quebec held unanimously that the board -should not have been established, because those who were applying for it were no longer in the service of the Street Railway Company. A decision directly opposite to that has been given by the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia. In that case, under one of the clauses of the Act, a man had been convicted for supplying food to strikers while they were on strike, contrary to the law. There is a section of the Act which prohibits any one aiding or abetting, and the court held that it was illegal to support men who had illegally gone- on strike. The matter came before the Appeal Court in Nova Scotia and the contention was put forward there that the Act did not apply to these men, because, as held in the Quebec case, they were no longer in the employ of their former employers, but the court in Nova Scotia held, that'within the meaning of the Act they were still employees. We therefore have a decision on both sides.	[DOT]

It was under the
Conciliation Act in Nova Scotia.

There was no board
there at all, and that is why it was illegal for them to strike. The conviction was sustained by the high court in Nova Scotia on the ground that although there was a strike, and they were no longer actually in the employ of their former employers, yet they still were employees within the meaning of the Act. These men who were to see me, did not ask, and never did ask for a board, but I casually told them of this decision, and that as I did not want to take any chances of another prohibition as in the Quebec case, I intended to propose to Parliament this session certain amendments which would become law sooner than an appeal from the judgment of the courts would likely be determined. It is not true that I ever at any time refused a board.
One hon. gentleman has read an extract from the Ottawa Citizen, and another hon. gentleman has read some sentences from a letter said to have been written by Mr. Frank Farrington. Well, I think we have all lived long enough to know that we should not place too much reliance on what we read in newspapers.
Hear, hear.

To my mind there are mis-statements in that article in the Ottawa Citizen; several important mis-statements. I hope my hon. friends opposite will not too seriously try to palm off on this House as gospel truth everything they can find in any newspaper. As I have said, some sentences were read from a letter sent me by Mr. Frank Farrington, and notwithstanding the observations made with reference to that gentleman by my hon. friend from Vancouver, I may say that there are a good many statements in that letter that I personally know to be untrue. I may say, further, that I wrote to this gentleman, as an officer' of the United Mine Workers of America, and pointed out to him-I think it was his chief the president who referred it to Farrington, but the reply came from Farrington-I pointed out that it was illegal to strike in this country until there was a board appointed, and asked him to make application for a board that we might have all the evidence before the public and an award given by an independent tribunal of three men. He wrote back that he was not breaking any Canadian law. That is the gentleman, part of whose letter to me was read by my hon. friend.
Then, some hon. gentleman opposite made

the statement that Mr. Price denied the men the right to appear before him. There is not a word of truth in that. I know that on one occasion Mr. Price had one hundred and twenty-five men before him and gave an invitation to each and every one of them to come forward and say anything he had to say touching the matter. On another occasion I was present when he had seventeen men before him, and on another occasion when he had forty men before him. There is no manner of foundation for the statement that he refused to hear anybody. Mr. Price is not a man of that kind; he is one of the most high-minded men we have in the country, and he is so regarded by every one who has the advantage of acquaintance with him.
There are some general observations which I might make with reference to the Labour Department. I have told you that during the first year I was in charge of it there were 900,000 less days lost in strikes than there were the year before. I may state now that for twenty years before I was placed in charge of the Labour Department there was on an average a strike in the coal mines of Nova Scotia every year. There has not been a strike in Nova Scotia in the coal mines since I came into office. There have not been any other labour disputes of any significance, and every one of them has been settled by boards established under the Industrial Disputes Act. When we came into power we found that strike out in the Crowsnest Pass going on for eight months. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) was in the House at that time, and so was my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell), and neither of them introduced any measure to amend the Industrial Disputes Act so as to settle that strike. The right hon. the leader of the Opposition was leader of the Government at that time, and there is no evidence that he suggested any additional legislation.

It was not necessary;
the existing legislation did the trick.

They were on strike
for eight months and it did the trick about a month after we came into power, but not before. My hon. friend, the Minister of Public Works, succeeded in getting put into that agreement a very important clause, and that was a provision that should any disputes subsequently arise within, I think five years, it would be decided by one man named in the agreement to act on behalf of the mine owners, and another man to act on behalf of the miners, and if these 36
two failed to agree on a third the Minister of Labour would appoint him.
Did the Minister of Public Works do that?

I understand he was
the means of getting that put into the agreement.

Then why
didn't you send him to British Columbia?

Under that agreement there have been several disputes settled in the Crowsnest Pass, and we have had no serious strike since it was entered into. My right hon. friend need not be too gay about sending the Minister of Public Works to Vancouver Island. There are some disputes more difficult to settle than others, as he has lived long enough to know. He was Prime Minister of this country for 22 months, during which there was a strike at Springhill, and he did not succeed in settling it.
He was here and saw the militia sent to three points in Nova .Scotia; yet he did not raise any disturbance about it. As far as concerns anything which has occurred since the rioting and unlawful acts on Vancouver Island, I am glad to know that the Government of British Columbia has recognized the fact that it is their duty to preserve law and order in all parts of that province, and I am very glad to know that they are vigorously performing their duty in that regard.

The
Minister of Labour seems to be under the belief or suspicion that members on this side of the House are conducting a concerted attack upon these votes in order to attack the minister himself. I am sure that there is no desire on the part of any member on this side of the House to deal unfairly with the Minister of Labour or -with the vote that he has passed, or is asking this committee to pass. All that this Committee wants is a fair and reasonable explanation by the minister of the part that he and his department have played in this very serious labour disturbance that has agitated the province of British Columbia and, in fact, practically the whole of Canada during the last year and a half. It seems to me that the minister has absolutely failed to meet the point of criticism from this side. Not only has he failed, but the hon. gentlemen from the province of British Columbia, who have undertaken to defend the minister



and his department" and to show that the minister has earned out his responsibility in a proper way in this matter, have absolutely failed to meet the real point of the criticism. The minister knows very well that in my country we do not believe in putting out a prairie fire after it has devastated forty or fifty miles of country; we believe that a prairie fire is such a dangerous thing that we must attack it right at the beginning or as near the beginning as possible.
I	take up this report of the special commissioner appointed by the minister, and what do I find? The minister says that we are somewhat previous in our discussions because we have not had certain returns brought down. So far as that is concerned, I might retort that the minister is previous in asking us to vote these sums of money until information, to which the House is entitled in connection with his department, is brought down.
From the somewhat incomplete report of a certain part of the events which took place on Vancouver Island in connection with this strike, what do we find in regard to the minister carrying out his responsibility as Minister of Labour, as the one upon whom devolves the responsibility of seeking to avert these unfortunate crises that sometimes arise between labour and capital? What evidence have we from the minister's own statement that he has actually seriously undertaken to carry out that responsibility? In the report of his special commissioner, so far as the inception of the trouble is concerned, we have one document signed by the Minister of Labour, that is the telegram in which he tells the contending parties on Vancouver Island, the mine owners and the miners, what their duty is under the Industrial Disputes Act. In other words, he tells them what they already know, that before striking they should have applied for a conciliation board.
In my judgment, the whole
II	p.m. trend of the Minister's statement is to the effect that the men were to blame for the strike. From the facts I do not find that the mine owners communicated with the minister or with the Department of Mines of the province of British Columbia in connection with the trouble, but I find in this report four communications, three addressed to the Minister of Labour at Ottawa and one addressed to the Premier of the province of British Columbia, in which representatives of the different

labour organizations addressed themselves to the minister to see if some way could not be found out of the serious difficulty in which those miners found themselves as the result of the disagreement between them and the mine owners. So far as I am concerned, the real essence of the criticism against the minister is the fact that, from the month of September, 1912, until the strike became general on the first of May, 1913, the minister, beyond sending the telegram pointing out to the miners of Vancouver Island what they already knew to be their duty under the Industrial Disputes Act, month by month sat still, realizing that the dispute was not settled, realizing that if it were not settled it must inevitably become worse as the disease spread.
I did not notice in the House last session that the Minister of Labour-we will call him that although he prefers, I understand, to be called by another name, the Minister of Play-was so acutely and actively busy that he could not have spared two or three weeks to take a trip last winter, instead of waiting until the following summer, to investigate the conditions that prevailed. Does not the minister himself think, does not any right-minded man in this House think that, when the first trouble commenced in the mines on Vancouver Island, the minister should have gone himself or sent his deputy or some man experienced in the settlement of disputes of that kind, preferably of course the Minister of Public Works, who is the wonder of the age, judging by what his colleagues say of his ability to settle strikes? If there was any time when he should have been busy in the settlement of the dispute, surely it was before the trouble became general and not when the minister went -out last July, when he found a situation which he himself could not control and with which he found it impossible to deal.
Having allowed the situation to go so far, and having allowed the strike to become general, what do we find the minister endeavouring to do? A general strike is called on the 1st of May. Surely the hon. minister must have had advance notice of it through his correspondents. If not, I wonder what these correspondents, who in different parts of the country are paid from $100 to $300 for furnishing reports to the Labour Gazette, which this House is asked to vote money to publish- I wonder what the correspondents in Van-

couver or Victoria were doing. If they did not furnish the hon. gentleman with information as to this strike, he ought to fire those correspondents and appoint men who would he alive to the situation. For here was a strike which threw hundreds of men out of employment, and with further trouble impending, yet the minister-tells us he knew nothing about it until the announcement was made that a general strike had been called by the President of the United Mine Workers of America.
The correspondent at Nanaimo, I may tell the hon. gentleman, is an appointee of the late Government.

If he is, and if he does not furnish better information than that tp which the minister refers, he ought to be fired. There is one decapitation which I can tell the hon. gentleman, we on this side will heartily endorse, if that is the way this man carries out his responsibility to the minister who is over him.
Now, when the general strike is called the minister seems to awaken out of the lethargic condition of somnolence which, apparently, like some animals, he enjoyed through the winter months. The session of Parliament over, the minister recommends the appointment of a Royal Commissioner to investigate the matter. I have no fault to find with this commissioner. I do not know anything about Mr. Price or his qualifications, but I have no reason to doubt his qualifications for the position. But I would like to ask this question: In the name of common sense what is the responsibility of the Minister of Labour, what is he appointed for by the Government? Why is there such a portfolio, why does this House vote the minister a salary year by year? Is it to sit in his office in Ottawa the year round, or to take pleasure trips to Europe or somewhere else? I have no fault to find with the minister fob taking a pleasure trip at the proper time. But why appoint a special commissioner to investigate a situation when he, as the member of the Government responsible "for the conduct of labour affairs was taking a trip to look into the situation? If I were a labouring man in Vancouver Island and saw the minister of the Crown who is responsible for looking after the interests of the workingman travelling to the seat of trouble in a private car accompanied by a gentleman to whom he had transferred a portion if not 361
all of his responsibility, I certainly should begin to wonder what sort of an administration was in charge of affairs in this thing. I say it is an extraordinary thing, it is anomalous, this appointment of a commissioner when the minister was going to the seat of trouble to investigite personally the state of affairs. I have here the report of the commissioner. I am not going to discuss it. It is somewhat extended and the commissioner's conclusions are general. Like the minister, he has come to the conclusion that nothing could be be done. When a man's house is afire, he may think it is a hopeless case and that the house will burn down, but surely he will struggle to preserve as much of his property as he can. But what do we find happens so far as the minister is concerned in the case? He comes back to the city of Ottawa and spends two or three weeks, I suppose in the supervision of his departmental affairs. Then, on the 13th of August, the press despatches contain the information that a serious condition has arisen in connection with the strike, that riots have occurred, that there is danger of loss of life and property. So serious is the matter that we find the militia are called out to maintain order. And in four days' time from that, we find the minister packing his grip and taking the first train out of Ottawa to put several thousand miles of briny ocean between him and the possible stray bullets from Vancouver Island that might reach the city of Ottawa. That may be the minister's view of the proper way to discharge his duty towards the workingmen of this country. But the workingmen, especially those in the province of British Columbia, must have heard with wonder the news that immediately the situation in Vancouver Island had become acute, the Minister of Labour packs his grip, takes the train out of Ottawa and presently is on the ocean on his way to have a little pleasure trip across the sea.
Perhaps I speak unfairly in referring to that as a pleasure trip; if I am not mistaken some one has suggested that the minister went to England to study industrial conditions and investigate conditions of labour across the sea. If the minister is prepared to get up in this House and say that the reason why he took this trip across the sea, when the real crisis of the trouble in British Columbia had been reached, was to find a solution for the labour problem in British Columbia, which, apparently, he could not find in this country, then he

would be offering some justification for his action. But I quite fail to understand how it was possible for the minister to manifest such absolute callousness and indifference in respect of this matter when the most serious crisis of the situation had been reached, by deliberately packing his grip and leaving on a trip to Europe. We have not had from the minister any report with regard to his trip to Europe. He is asking us to vote money to-night for the purpose of carrying on the work of his department. It has been said that the minister is asking for less than $100,000 whilst other ministers have the responsibility of spending larger sums. It may be quite true that the Minister of Labour is not responsible for the expenditure of a large sum of money, but I do maintain that he is the responsible head of one of the most important departments of this Government. The fact that he has the responsibility of dealing with labour disputes and of difficulties between employers and employees places upon the minister's shoulders a responsibility far greater, in my judgment, than the disbursement of money in public works. We are told that the minister went across the sea to study industrial conditions in England. There is one thing to be said in favour of the special commissioner who went to Vancouver Island; he did bring back a report, and we have it before us. I think the minister in asking for this vote should give the committee some insight as to the conclusions he arrived at as the result of his investigations in the old country. I am sure the committee would be delighted to know just what the minister discovered over there as to the best means of settling disputes of this nature. Did the minister actually look into labour conditions in England? Did he meet the labour leaders over there? Did he go down into the mines and collieries and study conditions there? Did he look into. conditions in the slums of London? I am sure we should all be glad to become acquainted with what the minister's trip to England means as far as any benefit to the people of this country is concerned. Is it the intention of the minister to bring down a report of this investigation? We are interested in this matter, because this country pays the minister for looking after his department. He has spent the money of this country not only in his trip across the continent to the province of British Columbia, but, I presume, also in his trip to Europe, and it is only fair that the minister should give us the information for which we are asking.

I wish to ask the minister if in his judgment he thinks that he used every proper and possible endeavour to prevent this strike in the province of British Columbia, which occurred in September, 1912, from becoming general, as it did, in the early part of May, 1913? That was the time to stop the trouble; did the minister take the necessary steps or put forth the needed efforts to bring about a cessation of trouble at that time? Everybody knows that a trouble of this kind, tackled at the proper time, is often very easily adjusted, but if it is allowed to grow for months and the passions of the contending parties are permitted to become inflamed by continuous friction and conflict, then it is very difficult to effect a remedy. I do not think that the minister ought to feel that he has been subjected to unfair criticism in this matter.
No, go on; I have no objection at all.

Did this Government
pay any portion, and if so what portion, of the expenses of the militia sent to Vancouver Island? Has the minister any well defined ideas in order to meet the various conditions that exist there at the present time?
I do not think our department has paid anything towards the expense of the militia.
Has this Government?
Not that I am aware of.
Not that I ever heard of.

It pays the difference
between what the officers and men would get when not on active duty and what they would get when they are on active duty.
The suggestion may be correct, but I am not sure. I would like to suggest that as the hour is late we should make a little progress, and then we might adjourn.

The Minister of Labour referred to the fact that there is a notice on the Order Paper which I intended to move asking for all papers and documents in connection with this matter. I do not think that I should have been called upon to make such a motion; I think the papers should have been brought down as soon as possible. My hon. friend has already brought down part of the record of his department in the report of the commission which he has appointed. This report, without the correspondence, is only part of the information we should have, and I would suggest to him that he bring down the papers before the next sitting of the committee.
I think my hon. friend from Humboldt is all out in saying that we have 39 on the staff now and that there were only 21 when we came into power.
Those are on the list.

I want to look up the list. Perhaps the hon. member for Humboldt was not here when I stated that we knew nothing about this strike at Cumberland until after it had actually occurred; we had no intimation whatever. By the first of May the mines at Cumberland were in operation and the output had grown to be almost normal. At every other mine on Vancouver Island there was an existing agreement between the men and their employers. Some of these agreements would not have lapsed for a year and a half more, and some would not have elapsed for six months more, so there was nothing to indicate that these men were not going to observe the terms of these agreements between the strike at Cumberland and the strike of the first of May, nothing whatever. If my hon. friend knew anything about labour movements he would know that men by the thousand may be called out in a few minutes by telegram. That is what happened in this case. A telegram sent, as I understand, from Seattle, calling out all these men who had no grievance against their employers and whose agreements with their employers had not expired. I had some 27 of these men before me and they admitted that they had entered into a written agreement. These were employees of the Western Fuel Company, of Nanaimo, and that agreement would not expire until the following October. They admitted that since that agreement had been entered into they had not made a single complaint to their employers. Yet, notwithstanding that, on a telegram from an officer of their association they quit work five or six months before the expiration of the agreement.
On account of the trouble at Cumberland.

Probably on account of the trouble at Cumberland, which was passing away. So we had no intimation of the strike until after it had occurred. Yet my hon. friend thinks we should have had a deputation out there watching all the time.

Would the minister not
know from the history and course of strikes?

No, it is not usual, it is very unusual to have these sympathetic strikes, and it is unusual for the men to break their agreement. The usual thing is that they carry out their agreement. As I said to them: You admit that you signed an agreement fixing the rates of wages and hours of labour; you admit that you never complained since that agreement was signed, and yet you went out on strike six months before the expiration of that agreement. That applies to all mines except those controlled by the Canadian Collieries. When the corespondence is brought down the hon. member for Humboldt will find that his statement that nothing was done except sending telegrams is absolutely without any foundation. I saw the man who controls the Cumberland mines, and my deputy went to Toronto to see another man, who is manager or next to the head man of the company that really controls those mines. We saw those men.
Let us see the correspondence.
We will let you see it when you get an order of the House.
Why not before?

It is not usual to
bring it down when there is a notice of motion.	'

It is usual to
bring any necessary information when you are asking for Supply.

I do not think it is
usual to bring all the corespondence you have in your office.

It is useful if it is not usual.
